displayQuote: A pint of sweat will save a gallon of blood

meta.title: Who really said "A pint of sweat will save a gallon of blood"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely George S. Patton: printed in his 1943 "Notes on Combat" in a War Department bulletin and reprinted in War As I Knew It (1947). Variants and older roots.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A pint of sweat will save a gallon of blood'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Patton. The exact line is in his 1943 "Notes on Combat" (War Department bulletin) and in War As I Knew It (1947). He called the idea an old rule.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Patton’s own “Notes on Combat,” printed in the War Department bulletin Tactical and Technical Trends, No. 30 (July 29, 1943), ends: “Remember that a pint of sweat will save a gallon of blood!” The line is reprinted in his War As I Knew It (1947). Patton wrote the line, but he himself called the idea an “old and sound rule.”

source.heading: Where Patton wrote it

docMeta.dd: “Notes on Combat,” by Lt. Gen. G. S. Patton Jr.
Tactical and Technical Trends, No. 30 (U.S. War Department), July 29, 1943
War As I Knew It (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1947), in the appendix of Letters of Instruction

source.excerpt: We can only conquer by attacking. In landing operations, continued ruthless pressure by day and by night is vital. In the initial phases of any campaign, we must be particularly emphatic in the ruthless destruction of the enemy. Remember that a pint of sweat will save a gallon of blood!
trail: July 29, 1943. Patton’s “Notes on Combat” is printed in the War Department’s Tactical and Technical Trends, No. 30. It ends “Remember that a pint of sweat will save a gallon of blood!” (Lone Sentry transcription ↗). This is the earliest printing we found.
June 5, 1944. In his speech to the Third Army, as transcribed, Patton gives a spoken variant: “I believe in the old and sound rule that an ounce of sweat will save a gallon of blood” (Wikiquote ↗).

1947. Houghton Mifflin publishes War As I Knew It after Patton’s death. Its reprinted Letters of Instruction contain the line, and Wikiquote’s sourced section cites the book for it (1947 edition at Internet Archive ↗; Wikiquote ↗).
source.excerptNote: The bulletin says these notes are extracts from a Patton letter of instruction to corps, division and separate brigade commanders, and from his report “Notes on Combat.” In War As I Knew It, the same sentence closes a combat principle in Letter of Instruction Number 2: “Your own fire reduces the effectiveness and volume of the enemy’s fire, while rapidity of attack shortens the time of exposure. A pint of sweat will save a gallon of blood!” The book’s narrative also uses a shorter form: “A pint of sweat saves a gallon of blood.” Wikiquote dates the letter 3 March 1944. The copy of the book text we checked dates Letter of Instruction Number 2 to 3 April 1944.

author.name: George S. Patton
author.heading: About George S. Patton
author.metaLine: 1885–1945 · U.S. Army general, commander of the Seventh and Third Armies in World War II
author.bio: George Smith Patton Jr. commanded U.S. forces in North Africa and Sicily. He then led the Third Army across France and into Germany in 1944–45. He was known for blunt, profane speeches and constant pressure on his commanders to keep moving. His wartime writings were published after his death in 1945 as War As I Knew It (1947).

misattribution.heading: Variants and look-alikes
misattribution.intro: This is a real Patton line, but it circulates in several versions and gets mixed up with similar military sayings credited to other people.

items.who: “An ounce of sweat will save a gallon of blood”
items.why: In the June 5, 1944 Third Army speech, as transcribed, Patton said “I believe in the old and sound rule that an ounce of sweat will save a gallon of blood.” It is the same idea from the same man, with “ounce” in place of “pint” (Wikiquote ↗).
Wikiquote notes a similar line attributed to Rommel: “Sweat saves blood, blood saves lives, and brains saves both.” It is a separate saying and should not be merged with Patton’s (Wikiquote ↗).

Wikiquote cites an older expression by Willich: “A drop of sweat on the drill ground will save many drops of blood on the battlefield,” from The Army: Standing Army or National Army? (1866) (Wikiquote ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The exact “pint of sweat” wording appears in Patton’s own 1943 notes and in his 1947 book (1943 text ↗). The underlying idea is older, and Patton called it an “old and sound rule.” It is not established that he coined the phrasing.

context.heading: Why Patton kept saying it
lead: For Patton, the line made a hard argument: drive troops harder in training and on the attack, and fewer of them die. The 1943 notes tie it to “continued ruthless pressure by day and by night.” In War As I Knew It, the same sentence closes a principle that casualties rise with the time troops spend exposed to enemy fire, so a fast attack is a safer one.

In the 1944 Third Army speech, as transcribed, he answers complaints that he pushed his men too hard: “The harder we push, the more Germans we will kill. The more Germans we kill, the fewer of our men will be killed. Pushing means fewer casualties” (Wikiquote ↗).

sourcesVerified.claim: Patton's "Notes on Combat" was printed in Tactical and Technical Trends, No. 30, July 29, 1943 (a U.S. War Department publication). It ends "Remember that a pint of sweat will save a gallon of blood!" and says the notes are extracts from a letter of instruction and a report by Lt. Gen. G. S. Patton Jr.

Wikiquote lists "A pint of sweat will save a gallon of blood" as Patton's, from a letter (3 March 1944) later published in War As I Knew It (1947). It transcribes the 5 June 1944 Third Army speech line "I believe in the old and sound rule that an ounce of sweat will save a gallon of blood" and "Pushing means fewer casualties." It notes similar sayings attributed to Rommel and to August Willich (The Army: Standing Army or National Army?, 1866).
Internet Archive record of War As I Knew It, by George S. Patton, published Boston, Houghton Mifflin Co., 1947 (borrow-only item).
George S. Patton was born 11 November 1885 and died 21 December 1945; he was a U.S. Army general.
